content.title: Is Masters champion Scottie Scheffler from New Jersey? Well, sorta ...
content.text: Pro & College SportsScottie Scheffler watches his tee shot on the 12th hole during the first round at the Masters golf tournament at Augusta National Golf Club Thursday, April 11, 2024, in Augusta, Ga.AP Photo/George Walker IVScottie Scheffler became just the 18th player in golf history to win a second Masters title on late Sunday afternoon at Augusta National, making him the kind of superstar athlete that everyone wants to claim as their own. So can we call him a Jersey Guy?Well, that might be a stretch. Scheffler was raised in the Dallas suburbs, after all, starring collegiately at Texas before beginning his professional career. He is far more likely to flash the “hook ‘em, Horns” hand signal than to flash the Tommy DeVito hand purse.Still: Scheffler has plenty of New Jersey ties. His father, Scott, grew up in Englewood Cliffs, and attended St. Cecilia High School, the high school where Vince Lombardi launched his coaching career. His mother, Diane, grew up in Park Ridge and was a classmate with the late James Gandolfini, one of the Jerseyiest celebrities of all time.Scheffler himself was born in Ridgewood and lived in Montvale for the first six years of his life. He took his first golf swings at Orchard Hills, a nine-hole track in Paramus, where his dad would hold up a flashlight and let his son pelt him with shots while his sister swam at the nearby Bergen Community College.“He used to hit us with the golf balls,” proud dad Scott Scheffler said at the 2022 Masters. “The police would kick us off, and we’d come back on, then the police would kick us off again. Then one day, the guy (at the course) finally came out and I said, ‘Could you just watch for a minute?’ And he’s like, ‘Wow. He’s really good at this!’ Then they wouldn’t bother us anymore.”But don’t listen to dad. One day before he slipped the green jacket on for the first time, I asked Scheffler directly: Can New Jersey claim you as one of ours? Not only did Scheffler answer yes, but he acknowledged that he listened to Bruce Springsteen, too, thanks to his pops.“They can (claim me) if they want to,” Scheffler answered. “I was born there. I lived there I think for (six) years. The only thing I remember was our backyard. I used to just hit golf balls in the backyard, hit them over the house. We had one of those (nets) you could throw the baseball against. Yeah, that’s where I spent most of my time was out in the yard, so that’s all I remember.”For Scheffler, this victory is more than just his second major championship. It confirms what everyone knew already, that the world’s No. 1 ranked player is far and away the dominant figure in the sport now, and at just 27, he figures to add several more majors to his resume before he’s through.So, yes, New Jersey should keep on claiming him as one of ours.“He’s born in New Jersey and raised in Texas, and he’s got a little bit of both in him,” dad Scott Scheffler said. “And that’s a good thing.”MORE FROM STEVE POLITI:N.J. gymnast Livvy Dunne is leading a revolution in college sportsThe untold story of how Rutgers crashed the Big TenHow an ex-Rutgers athlete ended up charged with murder in TijuanaI was a bird-flipping Little League menace — and it’s time to come cleanThe search for Luther Wright, once N.J.’s greatest hoops talentI played Augusta National and had my own Masters meltdownThank you for relying on us to provide the journalism you can trust.
